title: How did Arabia's highest virtue become a name of God?

beats.narration: What was the highest praise in old Arabia? Not brave. Not generous. Something quieter.

They called it hilm: the self-mastery of the man who holds his anger and does not rush to vengeance. Zuhayr paints the ideal chief in one stroke — forbearing in the assembly, fierce on the day of battle. A discipline, the poets said, you must school yourself into.

poetry.arabic: حُلَماءُ في النادي إِذا ما جِئتَهُم جُهَلاءُ يَومَ عَجاجَةٍ وَلِقاءِ
poetry.english: forbearing (ḥulamāʾ) in the assembly, fierce (juhalāʾ) on the day of battle-dust

beats.narration: The Quran inherits the virtue whole — and then moves its center of gravity. Here, the one who does not rush to punish rash words is God Himself: haleem. Forbearing. The chieftain's composure has become a divine name.
The poets kept forbearance while honor allowed and set it aside when honor demanded blood. Named of God, it loses that expiry date — restraint, not as strategy, but as who He is.
